covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: The manual does not define ‘very short’; reviewer resolution is needed before automating that exception.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory word, greeting or address lacks a separating comma, outside the very-short-sentence exception.
when: Except when the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-4: body gives the operative scope; G-2/G-3: short sentences are an exception.

covers.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase.

rules.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
rules.violation_condition: An introductory adverbial phrase or clause is not separated from the main clause by a comma.
when: Applies to introductory adverbial phrases and clauses, including conditional clauses.
A phrase moved to the end of the sentence does not require a preceding comma.
rules.why: G-2: conditional clauses are a case of the same introductory-clause check.

covers.quote: Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with an introductory date or number phrase immediately followed by another number.
when: An introductory phrase ending in a numeral is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.why: The structure preference is distinct from the punctuation required if that structure is used.

covers.quote: It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.

rules.quote: Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory phrase ends with a numeral and the following text begins with another numeral, without a separating comma.
when: Applies regardless of sentence length.
rules.why: A separately flaggable punctuation requirement, even when the discouraged structure is retained.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.specification: Check comma delimitation against whether the clause is essential: missing delimiters for supplementary clauses or inappropriate delimiters for essential clauses.
rules.violation_condition: A non-essential clause lacks its delimiting commas, or an essential clause is set off with commas.
when: A clause adds supplementary information or identifies/restricts the referent.
rules.why: G-1/G-2/G-4: the child rule includes the essential-clause contrast, not the grouping parent.

covers.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

rules.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
rules.violation_condition: A supplementary noun phrase defining the same thing as the preceding noun phrase is missing one or both delimiting commas.
when: The second noun phrase is supplementary and removable.
rules.why: G-4: heading and removal test elaborate the same apposition check.

covers.quote: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

rules.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A question tag is not preceded by a comma.
when: A question is tagged onto a sentence.
rules.why: G-1/G-4: retain the specific question-tag child, not its grouping parent.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.specification: Normally delimit medial ‘for example’ on both sides; at sentence start require only the following comma. A following bullet list instead takes a colon.
rules.violation_condition: ‘For example’ lacks a required delimiting comma in running text.
when: Except for the colon introducing a bullet list.
rules.why: G-2/G-4: sentence-initial placement is a case of the same delimitation check.

rules.quote: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list lead-in ending in ‘for example’ lacks a colon.
when: ‘For example’ introduces a bullet list.
rules.why: A colon introducing a list is a distinct finding from commas delimiting running text.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms

rules.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ is immediately followed by a comma.
rules.why: G-4: body specifies the prohibited comma position.

covers.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

rules.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
rules.violation_condition: Coordinated principal clauses lack separating commas where their subjects differ or where more than two clauses share a subject.
when: Require commas for clauses with different subjects.
Two clauses sharing a subject need no comma or repeated subject.
More than two principal clauses sharing a subject require separating commas.
rules.why: G-2/G-3: different subjects, shared subjects and three or more clauses are conditions of one check.

rules.quote: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence formed by joining principal clauses with commas and coordinating conjunctions exceeds 25 words.
when: Principal clauses are joined with commas and coordinating conjunctions.
rules.why: The explicit word limit is separately flaggable from conjunction punctuation.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: Two independent sentences are joined by a comma without a coordinating conjunction.
rules.why: G-4: body gives the operative comma-splice definition.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas

rules.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list.
rules.violation_condition: Items in a running sentence list lack separating commas.
when: Includes sentence lists within bullet-list fragments.
rules.why: G-1/G-4: specific list-separation check, not the grouping heading.

covers.quote: Restrict the use of the Oxford comma
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

rules.quote: Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
rules.specification: Flag an unnecessary serial comma or a missing serial comma needed to distinguish a compound final item or limit a defining phrase to that item.
rules.violation_condition: A list has an unnecessary comma before its final item, or lacks that comma when needed to distinguish the final item's internal coordination or defining phrase.
when: Use an Oxford comma when the final item itself contains ‘and’.
Use it to prevent ambiguity, including when a defining phrase applies only to the final item.
rules.why: G-2: Oxford-comma requirements and restrictions are cases of one final-item check.

rules.quote: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list item ends with a comma.
when: Applies to bullet lists.
rules.why: Bullet-ending punctuation is distinct from internal sentence-list separation.

rules.quote: When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
rules.violation_condition: Adjectives occur out of evaluative, descriptive, definitive order.
when: A string contains adjectives of different types.
rules.why: Adjective order is a separate textual property from comma placement.

covers.quote: Separate adjectives of the same type
Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

rules.quote: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).
rules.violation_condition: Adjacent adjectives of the same type lack a comma, or adjectives of different types have a separating comma.
when: Distinguish evaluative, descriptive and definitive adjectives.
rules.why: G-2/G-4: same-type and different-type cases determine one comma-placement check.

covers.quote: Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma. Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.
Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).
Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.
Don’t use commas in postcodes or dates.

rules.quote: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
rules.violation_condition: A numeral of at least 1,000 lacks correctly placed thousands commas or uses spaces instead; or a date, postcode or fractional digit sequence contains grouping commas.
when: Applies in text and tables.
Group integer digits in threes from right to left.
Do not group fractional digits, postcodes or dates.
rules.why: G-2/G-4: grouping, decimal digits, dates and postcodes are cases of one numeric-comma check.

rules.quote: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: Directly quoted speech follows its introductory attribution without a separating comma.
when: An attribution introduces directly quoted speech.
rules.why: G-1/G-4: body states a specific check beneath a grouping heading.

when: Directly quoted speech is introduced with a comma.

rules.quote: If an attribution comes after a quotation, use a comma at the end of the quotation and before the quotation mark.

when: The attribution follows the quotation.
rules.why: Following-attribution punctuation is distinct from introducing a quotation.
